title: Investing
description: Saving, investing, and why the years matter more than the perfect start.
wolfLine: Start smaller than you think, and earlier than you feel ready.

investing.definition: Buying something you expect to grow, or to pay you, over time. It can lose money too.
investing.example: Buying a fund and leaving it for years.

return.definition: The extra money an investment makes, or loses. A $1,000 investment that becomes $1,080 had an $80 return.

compound-growth.definition: Earning a return on your returns, not just on the money you put in.
compound-growth.example: A $1,000 investment that grows 10% two years in a row becomes $1,210, not $1,200.

rule-of-72.definition: A shortcut for how long money takes to double. Divide 72 by the yearly rate.
rule-of-72.example: At 6% a year, 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years to double.

stock.definition: A tiny piece of ownership in a company. If the company does well, your piece is worth more. It can also fall.
stock.example: Buying one share of a company for $40.

bond.definition: A loan you make to a government or a company. They pay you interest and, at the end, your money back.
bond.example: Lending $1,000 to the government for ten years.

risk.definition: The chance an investment loses money, or swings wildly, before you need it.
risk.example: A stock that might be up 20% or down 20% in a year.

dividend.definition: Cash some companies pay their owners out of profits. Not every stock pays one.
dividend.example: A $40 stock that pays $1 a year.

portfolio.definition: Everything you own as investments, taken together.
portfolio.example: Some stocks, some bonds, and a fund.

lessons.title: Compound Growth
lessons.summary: Money that earns money on its money.

steps.context: [[Investing]] means buying something you expect to grow, or to pay you, over time. The extra you make is your [[return]]. You can lose money too.
steps.prompt: You invest $1,000 and a year later it’s worth $1,080. What’s the extra $80?
steps.explain: The extra is your [[return]]: $1,080 − $1,000 = $80.

steps.prompt: You invest $2,000 and earn a 10% return in a year. What’s it worth now?

steps.context: [[Compound growth]] means you earn a return on the returns too, not just on the money you first put in.
steps.prompt: Your $1,000 grew to $1,100. Next year, you’ll earn a return on…
steps.explain: [[Compound growth]] means next year’s return is on the whole pile, not just the start.

steps.prompt: That $1,100 earns another 10% in year two. What’s it worth now?
steps.explain: $1,100 × 1.10 = $1,210. The second year’s return is $110, not $100.

steps.context: The [[rule of 72]] is a shortcut. Divide 72 by the yearly rate to see about how many years a pile takes to double.
steps.prompt: Roughly how many years does it take to double your money at 6% a year?
steps.explain: The [[rule of 72]]: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. It’s a rough guide, not a promise.

steps.prompt: Starting to invest 10 years earlier can matter more than investing a bigger amount later.
steps.explain: Time is the fuel. The early years do a lot of the compounding.

lessons.title: Stocks and Bonds
lessons.summary: Own a piece, or lend your money.

steps.context: A [[stock]] is a tiny piece of a company. If the company does well, your piece can be worth more. It can also fall.
steps.prompt: What is a stock?
choices: A tiny piece of a company
steps.explain: A [[stock]] is ownership. You share in the company’s wins and losses.

steps.context: A [[bond]] is a loan you make to a government or a company. They pay interest, and at the end they pay the loan back.
steps.prompt: What is a bond?
choices: A loan to a government or a company
steps.explain: A [[bond]] is a loan you make. They pay you interest, then your money back.

steps.context: [[Risk]] is the chance you lose money, or the value swings hard, before you need the cash. Stocks usually swing more than bonds or savings.
steps.prompt: Which usually swings more in a given year?
steps.explain: [[Risk]] is the chance of a loss or a wild swing. Stocks usually swing more than a savings account.

steps.context: A [[dividend]] is cash some companies pay their owners out of profits. Not every stock pays one.
steps.prompt: What is a dividend?
choices: A fee the company charges you
Cash some companies pay their owners
steps.explain: A [[dividend]] is a share of profits paid out. Plenty of stocks pay none.

steps.context: A [[portfolio]] is everything you own as investments, taken together.
steps.prompt: What is a portfolio?
choices: All of your investments, taken together
steps.explain: Your [[portfolio]] is the whole mix, not one piece.

steps.prompt: Match each word with what it is.
You’ll need your money in one year for a house deposit. What fits better?
choices: Mostly safe, steady places like a savings account
steps.explain: Stocks can drop right before you need the cash. A short timeline wants less risk.

lessons.title: Saving or Investing
lessons.summary: Soon money and later money do different jobs.

steps.title: Two jobs
steps.body:
Saving keeps money steady for a bill you can already see. [[Investing]] is for money you can leave alone for years. The [[return]] can be larger, and it can also be a loss.

A savings account’s [[APY|apy]] is the yearly rate it pays you. That rate is the steady kind.

docs.title: Cash for a move in eight months
docs.subtitle: A savings account

docs.title: Money for a goal 25 years away
docs.subtitle: An investment account
docs.note: The $80 is an example return, not a promise.

steps.prompt: You need this $1,000 in eight months. Which page is the better home for it?
choices: Cash for a move in eight months
Money for a goal 25 years away
steps.explain: Eight months is soon. A drop would matter. The 25-year page can ride out a bad year. The $80 there is an example, not a promise.

steps.prompt: The savings page pays 4% APY on $1,000. How many dollars of interest is that in a year?
steps.explain: $1,000 × 0.04 = $40. That is the savings return in this example.

steps.prompt: Money you invest can be worth less than you put in.
steps.explain: A higher possible return comes with the chance of a loss. Savings is the steadier job.

steps.prompt: Which pile is a better fit for money you will not need for 25 years?
choices: The savings page, because it cannot grow
The investing page, because decades can ride out drops
Whichever one paid more last month
steps.explain: A long timeline is what makes the swings bearable. Last month is not a plan.

lessons.title: Risk and Return
lessons.summary: The wider swing is the price of the higher chance.

steps.title: The trade
steps.body: A savings account barely moves. A [[stock]] can move a lot. That wider [[risk]] is why stocks have, historically and on average, paid more than savings over many decades. It is not a promise for any one year.

steps.prompt: Which has the wider range of outcomes in a single year?
choices: They are locked to the same result
steps.explain: Stocks can rise a lot or fall a lot. That range is the risk.

steps.prompt: A $1,000 stock investment falls 20% in a year. How many dollars did it lose?
steps.explain: $1,000 × 0.20 = $200. It is worth $800. A bad year is part of the deal.

steps.prompt: A chance of a higher return means the investment cannot lose money.
steps.explain: The higher chance and the chance of a loss come together.

steps.prompt: A tuition bill is due in ten months. Where should that tuition money sit?
choices: In a savings account you can count on
In whatever rose the most last year
steps.explain: Ten months is a short timeline. A drop would hit the bill. Keep that cash steady.

lessons.title: Time in the Market
lessons.summary: Staying in has done more than jumping around.

steps.title: Stay on the ride
steps.body: Historically, on average, the gains have come in bursts. Sitting out to dodge a drop often means missing the rebound too. The habit that has worked is time in the market: stay invested, and keep adding.

steps.prompt: You are investing for 30 years and the market has a bad month. What fits the long habit?
choices: Sell everything and wait for calm
Keep the plan and keep adding
Move it all into the one stock that fell the least
steps.explain: A bad month is not a 30-year result. Staying in is the habit.

steps.prompt: Selling after a drop locks that drop in.
steps.explain: Once you sell, the lower price is the price you took. Staying in leaves the chance of a recovery.

steps.prompt: Your plan is $100 a month. You skip six months because you are scared. How many dollars did you not add?
steps.explain: 6 × $100 = $600. Those deposits never got the later years of compounding.

steps.prompt: The long habit is called time in the ___.
steps.explain: Time in the market means staying invested. Timing means trying to jump in and out.

lessons.title: The Cost of Waiting
lessons.summary: Ten quiet years are not free.

steps.title: What the wait skips
steps.body: Waiting does two things. You skip the deposits, and you skip the years those deposits could compound. This lesson uses an example rate of 8% a year. It is an example, not a promise.

steps.prompt: You can invest $50 a month. How many dollars is that in one year?
At $50 a month, how many dollars do you deposit over 10 years, before any growth?
steps.explain: 10 × $600 = $6,000. Waiting ten years means those deposits never happen.

steps.prompt: Using the rule of 72, about how many years does an example 8% rate take to double?
steps.explain: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. About, and only at that example rate.

steps.prompt: An example 8% doubles $1,000 in about 9 years, to $2,000. How many of those dollars are growth?
steps.explain: $2,000 − $1,000 = $1,000 of growth. If you wait the 9 years and only then invest $1,000, that growth never starts.

steps.prompt: Waiting to invest is free, because you can always start later with the same result.
steps.explain: Later skips both the deposits and the years of compounding. The wait has a cost.

lessons.title: Emergency Fund First
lessons.summary: Investing comes after the cash pile.

steps.title: Cash, then investing
steps.body: An [[emergency fund]] is cash for a surprise, not an investment. A drop in the market is a bad week to also lose your job. Fill the cash pile before you invest extra money.

doc.title: Cash on hand
doc.subtitle: Keep the emergency fund invested in nothing

steps.prompt: On this page, how many dollars are the extra cash you could invest?
steps.explain: The extra cash is $400. The $1,000 emergency fund stays put.

doc.title: Cash on hand
doc.subtitle: Keep the emergency fund invested in nothing

steps.prompt: How many dollars stay in the emergency fund?
steps.explain: That $1,000 is for a surprise. It is not the investing pile.

steps.prompt: The emergency fund should be your first investment in stocks.
steps.explain: The emergency fund stays in cash. You invest money you can leave alone.

steps.prompt: Why not invest the emergency fund?
choices: Because you may need it in a month when stocks are down
Because cash earns more than stocks
steps.explain: The fund has to be there on a bad day. A stock drop and a surprise bill together is the problem it prevents.

lessons.title: Lily Starts Small
lessons.summary: Fifty dollars is a real start.

story.title: Fifty dollars a month
story.body:
Lily takes home about **$2,200** a month. She already keeps **$1,000** in savings as an emergency fund.

After rent and food she can spare **$50** a month. She will invest that, and she will not touch the $1,000.

steps.title: Meet Lily
steps.body:
Lily is 23 and a cafe shift lead. She takes home about $2,200 a month. She already has a $1,000 [[emergency fund]] in savings. After rent and food she can spare $50 a month.

She will not invest the $1,000. She will invest the $50, automatically, and leave it alone.

steps.prompt: How many dollars does Lily invest in a year at $50 a month?
steps.explain: 12 × $50 = $600. Small, and it is a start.

steps.prompt: If she keeps that up for 10 years, how many dollars has she deposited, before any growth?
steps.explain: 10 × $600 = $6,000. The growth, if it comes, is on top of that.

steps.prompt: Lily should move the $1,000 emergency fund into stocks so the account looks bigger.
steps.explain: The $1,000 has a job. A surprise bill should not depend on the market.

steps.prompt: Put Lily’s start in order.
items: Keep the $1,000 emergency fund in cash
steps.explain: Cash first, then the automatic deposit, then patience.

lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.
